arguments.heading: What happened at the argument
paragraphs: Mr. Johnson argued that the specific facts of the 1978 conviction do not matter.
He stated that only the statutory definition matters for the Armed Career Criminal Act.
Justice Scalia asked if state supreme court statements about weapon types suffice for classification.
Justice Alito questioned whether two different phrasings of an element are substantively equivalent.

sections.heading: What this case is about
paragraphs: This case tests the limits of the categorical approach. It asks if federal courts can look beyond the statutory text to state court decisions. The outcome affects how judges count prior offenses for sentencing enhancements.

paragraphs: The Supreme Court heard oral argument in this case on January 7, 2013.

sections.heading: What each side wants
paragraphs: the side that brought the case wants the Supreme Court to limit federal courts to the statutory text alone.
The government wants the Supreme Court to allow courts to use state court interpretations to define elements.

sections.heading: What each side says
paragraphs: the side that brought the case argues that federal courts must ignore state court opinions when applying the categorical approach.
The government argues that state supreme court interpretations clarify the elements of the underlying state offense.

sections.heading: What the justices asked
paragraphs: Justice Kagan asked if the Ninth Circuit could reimagine any indivisible statute as having divisible elements.
Justice Alito asked if there is a difference between an element and a violation of a possessory interest.
